title: Curve instances extend the rate-limit schema with a third leg for swaps and a non-quantity parameter for slippage
content:
Every Curve Instance Configuration Document restates its `Rate Limits` header differently from the rest of the Artifact: "The current `maxAmount`, `slope` and slippage for this conduit's inflow/outflow/**swap**" (A.6.1.1.1.2.6.1.3.1.7.1.2.4, and identically at .7.2.2.4, .7.3.2.4, .7.4.2.4, .7.5.2.4, .7.6.2.4). Each then carries three children — `Inflow`, `Outflow` and `Swap Rate Limits` — and most legs add a `Max slippage` line, e.g. the sUSDS/USDT pool's swap limits: "`maxAmount`: 10,000,000, `slope`: 200,000,000 per day, Max slippage: 0.25%" (.7.1.2.4.3).

Two extensions are happening at once. The first is structural: a two-legged conduit model becomes three-legged, because an AMM supports an action — swapping — that is neither depositing nor withdrawing and that leaves the balance sheet's size unchanged while changing its composition.

The second is more significant. `maxAmount` and `slope` bound *how much* moves; `Max slippage` bounds *at what price*. Every other risk parameter in the Spark Liquidity Layer is a volume throttle, which is the right control when the risk is counterparty exposure. For a swap the exposure is momentary and the real hazard is execution quality — an adverse pool state, thin liquidity, or a sandwich attack — none of which a volume cap addresses.

Adding slippage therefore admits that the quantity-only model of risk does not generalise. It also means Curve conduits fail differently: an oversized swap is rejected by the rate limit, but a badly priced one is rejected by the slippage bound, and only the second protects against losing value on a trade that was perfectly legal by size.
description: Where lending venues have inflow and outflow, every Curve instance adds Swap Rate Limits and a Max slippage bound — the first control in the schema that governs execution price rather than volume.
